source.title: Sparse Autoencoders Do Not Find Canonical Units of Analysis
source.authors: Patrick Leask; Bart Bussmann; Michael Pearce; J. Bloom; Curt Tigges; N. A. Moubayed; Lee Sharkey; Neel Nanda

record.tranche_reason: The study reports its own SAE-stitching and meta-SAE results that refine feature-splitting claims and challenge the idea that any SAE width yields a complete, atomic dictionary.
record.gate_note: The study directly compares SAE dictionaries of different sizes using stitching and analyzes larger-SAE decoder directions with meta-SAEs. Its discussion of broad mathematical features splitting into narrower ones is attributed to prior work, so that cited example is not recorded as a result. Sparse-probing and concept-removal results do not measure the claim versions.
record.test_reason: The study compares GPT-2 SAEs of 768 to 98304 latents and two Gemma Scope SAEs using stitching and meta-SAEs. Its results bear on V1 (some latents split, others compose) and V5. It is an original source for V5, so V5 gets no verdict here.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors also attribute the non-atomic, composed latents to the sparsity penalty. They state that their methods do not identify canonical units or the right dictionary size.
record.recipe_differences: The study compares different dictionary sizes trained on model activations, but uses its own stitching procedure based on decoder cosine similarity and a meta-SAE trained on decoder directions rather than directly checking whether child features partition a coarse feature's inputs.
record.method_sensitivity: The cosine threshold differs by SAE family: 0.7 for GPT-2 SAEs and 0.4 for Gemma Scope SAEs.

fits_no_version.finding: Larger-SAE latents are often compositions of smaller-SAE latents (e.g. Einstein = scientist + Germany + famous). Swapping lowers L0, and the authors attribute this to the sparsity penalty.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Growing the dictionary merges independent features into composed latents (feature composition), the converse of splitting. Attributed to the sparsity penalty but not tested against other objectives.

record.problems: The study tests only two LLMs and acknowledges that it does not include very large SAEs. Stitching classifies latents using exploratory cosine-similarity thresholds. The reported size-comparison figures generally do not provide numerical values in the text, and the study does not show that split features partition the same inputs.
record.rows_left_out: No additional claim-relevant result rows were left out. Results in Appendix A.8 on sparse probing and concept removal do not test the listed claim versions.

untested.parts: Whether child latents jointly cover the parent's inputs. Only decoder cosine similarity is used (activation similarity only in Figure 8).
Splitting itself is not examined in Gemma Scope or in large models. Only novel-versus-reconstruction stitching was run on Gemma 2 2B.
Hierarchical nested families are not tested.
Composition is attributed to the sparsity penalty but no alternative objective is compared.

missing.what: Same-size SAEs from different seeds: 94% of latents are reconstruction latents (cosine >0.7).
Averaged over the 657 novel GPT2-1536 latents, the smaller SAE's MSE is worse where those latents are active.
Adding all GPT2-1536 latents with cosine ≤0.7 to GPT2-768 reduces MSE by almost 10%.
Swapping reconstruction latents generally increases MSE but almost always decreases L0. This conflicts with R2's reading of Figure 5.
Decoder cosine similarity vs activation similarity: R²=0.87 at cosine >0.5.

record.verdict_notes: This study is an original source for V5, so V5 has no labels. Its stitching uses exploratory cosine thresholds (0.7 for GPT-2, 0.4 for Gemma). Most size results are figure-only.

versions.untested_parts: The study does not establish that split features jointly cover the same inputs as a coarse feature.
Tests GPT-2 Small and Gemma 2 2B, not very large models or other SAE families beyond the tested Gemma Scope releases.
Nested families mirroring a hierarchy of concepts are not tested.
Parent-child firing failures and whether size or sparsity changes fix them are not tested.
The study does not establish that all larger latents decompose into smaller latents or that any particular dictionary lacks all useful atomic units.
The study does not compare SAE objectives, test Matryoshka SAEs, or isolate whether the objective rather than model representations causes the reported structure.

relation.reason: Its own results bear on V1 and V5.

tranche.reason: Different method (stitching, meta-SAE) on the same question, and it argues larger-SAE latents compose rather than only split.

source_check.notes: V5 gets no verdict (original source). Figure 5/Section 4.2 say swaps improve MSE on average; Figure 14 says individual swaps generally raise MSE (outliers hidden); the text does not reconcile them. GPT-2 SAEs span 768 to 98304; Gemma Scope pair is layer 12; Figure 13 sweeps the threshold (ROC).

statements.correction: Figure 5 caption: both steps on average improve reconstruction (MSE). Section 4.2: each step on average improves reconstruction. Appendix A.6, Figure 14: swapping latent structures generally increases MSE, almost always decreases L0, outliers not shown. The text does not reconcile the two.
statements.problem: Calls swaps improving MSE R2's reading of a figure, contrasted with r13 'stated in the text'. The paper itself states it in the Figure 5 caption and Section 4.2. Figure 14 covers per-swap effects with outliers hidden, so this is an unreconciled tension, not a shown contradiction.

statements.correction: arXiv:2502.04878: 657 GPT2-1536 latents have low max cosine to GPT2-768; some reconstruction latents compose several smaller-SAE latents.
statements.problem: The 35% novel figure comes from the stitching post, not this paper. The paper gives 657 novel latents in GPT2-1536 (about 43% of 1536) and does not state 35%.

statements.correction: arXiv:2502.04878 Appendix Figure 13: ROC curve from varying the max-cosine threshold for classifying novel vs reconstruction latents against the sign of the MSE effect (figure only, no AUC stated). Figure 4: MSE change per GPT2-1536 latent vs max cosine to GPT2-768. Thresholds 0.7/0.4 were set from exploratory analysis.
statements.problem: Says no study reports V5 outcomes at several thresholds. This paper sweeps the cosine threshold in an ROC curve for predicting whether adding a latent lowers MSE, and plots every latent's MSE change against max cosine.

statements.correction: R1: adding novel latents improves MSE on average; R3: adding them raises average L0. GPT-2 Small layer-8 SAEs: 768 to 98,304 latents (stitching chain in Figure 5: 768 to 12288; meta-SAE on the 49152 SAE). Figure 5 caption and Section 4.2 say swaps improve MSE on average. Figure 14: individual swaps generally increase MSE (outliers not shown). The text does not reconcile the two.
statements.problem: R3 is cited for MSE, but R3 is the L0 increase. Settings say GPT-2 SAEs span 768 to 12288; the paper's eight SAEs span 768 to 98304. The statement also frames swaps improving MSE as R2's reading, though the paper states it in the Figure 5 caption and Section 4.2.
